title: How to split a taxi fare fairly
description:
Three friends share a cab and the meter reads 6 euros at the first stop, 18 at the second, 30 at the last. Split evenly, the first one out pays 10 for a ride that costs 6 alone. The fair way: cut the ride at every stop and split each stretch only among the people still in the car: 6 / 3 = 2 each, then 12 / 2 = 6 each, then the last 12 for the last rider. That gives 2, 8 and 20, and it's exactly what you get by averaging, over all 6 orders the riders could join, the extra driving each one adds: the Shapley value. Littlechild and Owen showed in 1973 that the same rule, proposed for airport runway landing fees, is the Shapley value.

Numbers checked in code: every share computed exactly, plus 200,000 simulated random join orders (2.00, 8.00, 20.00). Sources: Wikipedia, Airport problem and Shapley value; Littlechild & Owen, Management Science 20(3), 1973.

facts_checked: Meter 6 / 18 / 30: even split 10 each; stretch rule 6/3 = 2, 12/2 = 6, 12/1: you 2, Ben 8, Mia 20; equals the Shapley value averaged over all 6 join orders; 200,000 simulated random orders give 2.00 / 8.00 / 20.00; CTA meter 12, 24, 36, 48 -> 3, 7, 13, 25 (verify.py)

Airport problem: runway cost shared by aircraft needing different lengths; each increment of runway is split equally among the landings that need it, and the resulting charges are the Shapley value; introduced by S. C. Littlechild and G. Owen, 'A Simple Expression for the Shapley Value in a Special Case', Management Science 20(3), 1973 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airport_problem)
Littlechild & Thompson (1977) applied the runway cost-sharing game to Birmingham Airport, 1968-69, with Shapley-value landing fees (https://ideas.repec.org/a/rje/bellje/v8y1977ispringp186-204.html)

beats.say: Your 6 euro taxi ride costs 10, split evenly.
Paying the meter at your stop isn't fair either. All three of you rode that stretch.
The meter reads 6 at your stop, 18 at Ben's, 30 at Mia's.
Cut the ride at every stop. Split each stretch only among who's still in the car. First 6: three riders, 2 each.
Next 12: two riders, 6 each. The last 12 is all Mia's.
You pay 2. Ben, 8. Mia, 20. Mia says it's rigged.
So try all 6 orders you could have joined the ride. Each person pays the extra driving they add. Average it: 2, 8, 20.
That's the Shapley value. Runways can be priced the same way: every plane shares the first stretch, only jumbos pay for the end.
